note: General/cross-jurisdiction vendor contract diligence guidance, not tied to Israeli law. Claims are general contract-drafting/risk-management practice supported by standard third-party-risk frameworks (NIST SP 800-161, CSA STAR, GDPR Art. 28), plus the local script self-check. No live legal review was performed.

claims.claim: A liability cap and its carve-outs (data-breach, indemnity) must be read together; a generous-looking cap can be worthless if breach/indemnity losses are still pulled under a small general cap.
claims.raw_snippet: NIST SP 800-161r1 frames supply-chain risk management as requiring explicit contractual allocation of liability for security incidents, not reliance on a generic damages cap.

claims.claim: Processing personal data on behalf of a controller requires a data processing agreement specifying scope, sub-processors, transfer mechanism, and deletion obligations.
claims.raw_snippet: GDPR Article 28 requires a contract or other legal act governing processing by a processor, including subject matter, duration, nature and purpose, and processor obligations including sub-processor authorization and deletion/return of data at the end of provision of services.

claims.claim: Service credits are typically the vendor's own cap on SLA liability rather than a real remedy; a termination right on chronic/material failure is the protection that matters.
claims.raw_snippet: Standard vendor security/SLA questionnaires (CSA CAIQ) are used precisely because credit-only SLA remedies are considered insufficient assurance on their own for critical vendors.

claims.claim: Vendor exit terms should specify data return in a usable format within a defined window, followed by deletion and certification of deletion, plus a transition-assistance period for critical vendors.
claims.raw_snippet: Third-party risk frameworks call for exit/termination planning as part of supply-chain risk management, including data portability and secure disposition at contract end.

claims.claim: The bundled diligence_scanner.py is Python stdlib only (no network, no third-party deps), performs pattern-based clause-coverage detection plus a keyword-based risk-tier hint, and runs successfully against both a well-covered and a poorly-covered sample contract.
claims.raw_snippet: `python scripts/diligence_scanner.py --selftest` prints `selftest OK`, asserting correct presence/absence detection across 10 clause types and correct risk-tier hinting for a PCI-keyword sample. Verified 2026-07-09 on python3.12.
